passage: Wei printed three pages before dinner in Vancouver: graduate figures from a design school, the starting pay listed on its site, and a plan. Wei's mother, Xin, expected engineering, like Wei's uncle. "I know you worry about jobs," Wei began, hands not quite steady. "Here is the share of last year's design graduates who were in work. And here is a course at the same university that mixes engineering and design, if you'd rather have both." Xin scanned the pages in silence. "One term," Wei said. "Let me take the design elective and keep science. If my science marks drop, we talk again." Xin folded her reading glasses. "Show me the elective's timetable," she said at last.

qa.q: What three things did Wei print before dinner?
qa.a: Wei printed graduate figures from a design school, the starting pay listed on its site, and a plan.

qa.q: What is Wei feeling as the talk begins, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Wei is nervous but determined; the hands not quite steady and the careful preparation show it.

qa.q: Which part of Wei's approach makes agreement easier, and why?
qa.a: The one-term trial with science kept: it is small and can be undone, so Xin risks little.

qa.q: What might Xin be worried about?
qa.a: Wei's job prospects, since Xin expected engineering like Wei's uncle; asking for the timetable shows Xin is taking the plan seriously.

grounding: Wei wants design while the family expects engineering, and presents real paths, numbers and a trial term.

passage:
Chinmay, you think your parents are the first to say "only science"? Sit, let me tell you, it's your Maria Aunty's turn to lecture.

In Class 10, I wanted design. Fashion, textiles, all of it. My father wanted engineering like my three cousins. For a month I sulked. Barely ate at dinner. Went to my room and slammed the door.

Then my teacher said something I never forgot: "Sulking isn't an argument, Maria." So I went to the library and the career fair. I wrote down what design graduates from the city college were doing: which companies, how many got jobs in the first year. I talked to a woman who ran a textile studio in Bandra.

I sat my father down with two pages of notes. I asked for one trial year: design classes on weekends, science in school. If I hated it or failed science, I'd stop.

He read it twice. He said yes. Your Maria Aunty has been a textile designer for thirty years.

qa.q: What did Maria Aunty's teacher say to her?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Sulking isn't an argument, Maria."

qa.q: What was young Maria feeling during the month she sulked?
qa.a: Young Maria felt frustrated and resentful, which is why she barely ate at dinner and slammed her door.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Researching real design paths and asking her father for a one-year trial turned things around, because it gave him facts and a safe limit instead of sulking.

qa.q: How might Maria's father have felt reading the two pages of notes?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and reassured to see she had done serious research, which helped him say yes.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling wanting design while her family expected engineering, and how research, facts and a trial period worked better than sulking.

The stream form was due at nine the next morning. At eleven at night, Nirmala was still sitting on the floor of the room she shared with her elder sister Bidisha, the form blank on her knee.

"Humanities, with psychology and fine arts," she said. "That's what I want. Papa will say only science."

"Then don't just say it," Bidisha said. "Show him."

They had one laptop, a bad connection and two hours. Bidisha looked up the design colleges in their state; Nirmala wrote down admission routes, entrance tests, and three careers alumni had gone into. Bidisha found the school's rule: students could switch streams within the first month.

At seven, over tea, Nirmala put the sheet in front of her parents. "I want humanities. Here's what it leads to. And if I'm struggling after one month, I'll switch to science, the school allows it."

Papa read, frowning. "One month."

"One month."

He signed the form.

qa.q: When was the stream form due?
qa.a: The stream form was due at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she sat with the blank form?
qa.a: Nirmala felt anxious and stuck, sure of what she wanted but worried Papa would only accept science.
Researching real paths with Bidisha, writing down admission routes and careers, and offering a one-month trial made her case stronger than just asking.

qa.q: How might Papa see the one-month offer?
qa.a: Papa may feel reassured that there is a way back to science, which makes it easier for him to agree.

grounding: It shows a teen who wants arts while her family expects science, who researches real paths under time pressure and asks for a trial period instead of sulking.
